Last updated: 2026-11-17

**COMPROMISED: standard pointing does not mark whether a shva is pronounced (the rules decide it from the shape of the word, which is right for most words but not all); qamats qatan is mostly not distinguished from qamats**

# Background

**Language Family:** Afro-Asiatic / Semitic / Central / Northwest / Canaanite

* These rules describe Modern Israeli Hebrew, as read from **pointed** text, that is, text written with the vowel diacritics (*niqqud*). Hebrew is normally written without them. Unpointed spelling leaves most vowels unwritten: *sefer* 'book' and *safar* 'count' are both written ספר [@gafter_performing_2019]. That much ambiguity is beyond what XPF rules can resolve, so only pointed text is covered.
* Even pointed text does not fully determine Modern Hebrew pronunciation. The pointing system was not designed for Modern Hebrew: it makes more vowel distinctions than the language has, and some diacritics stand for two Modern Hebrew vowels [@gafter_performing_2019]. The places where this matters for the rules are listed under **Alphabet**.
* The rules come from the he2ipa project, which remains their source: the corpus copy is updated from he2ipa, not edited here. They work on plain pointed text, with two input conventions:
    - a prefix (ו, ה, ב, כ, ל, מ, ש) must be followed by `|`, as in וּ|מַיִם or הַ|יְּלָדִים. Without it the prefix rules do not apply and the word gets the classical reading;
    - input may be in either Unicode normalization form (NFC or NFD);
    - optional marks override the defaults: meteg (U+05BD) forces a heard shva, ole (U+05AB) marks lexical stress, and rafe (U+05BF) keeps ב, כ or פ a fricative after a prefix (in loanwords).
* Where speakers differ, the rules follow the conservative reading that the spelling encodes, such as keeping the pharyngeals. Users who want another variety can change the output with a final `ipasub` rule (see **Consonants**).

# Phonology

## Consonants

| Manner | Labial | Alveolar | Postalveolar | Palatal | Velar | Uvular | Pharyngeal | Glottal |
|:--|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **Stops** | p b | t d | | | k ɡ | | | ʔ |
| **Affricates** | | ts | tʃ dʒ | | | | | |
| **Fricatives** | f v | s z | ʃ ʒ | | | χ | ħ ʕ | h |
| **Nasals** | m | n | | | | | | |
| **Rhotic** | | | | | | ᴚ | | |
| **Approximants** | w | l | | j | | | | |

*Voiceless on the left, voiced on the right. For a phonetic description of the consonants and vowels, see @asherov_cohen_2019.*

* **Rhotic.** The rhotic is transcribed /ᴚ/ in every word. Its realization varies between speakers and positions, from a uvular fricative or approximant to an alveolar tap or trill [@cohen_laks_savu_2019; @gafter_modern_2019], and /ᴚ/ names the phoneme without choosing among them. To get a specific symbol, add an `ipasub` rule that replaces it everywhere, with a weight below every other rule in the file (for example `{from: ᴚ, to: ʁ, weight: 0}`).
* **Pharyngeals.** ח and ע are transcribed /ħ/ and /ʕ/. Most speakers merge /ħ/ with /χ/ and /ʕ/ with /ʔ/ (or drop it) [@gafter_horesh_2020; @faust_gutturals_2019]. The pharyngeals are kept mainly by Mizrahi speakers, for whom they carry social meaning [@gafter_whats_2016; @gafter_modern_2019]. A merged variety can be produced the same way as above, with final `ipasub` rules from /ħ/ to /χ/ and from /ʕ/ to /ʔ/.
* **/w/, /dʒ/, /tʃ/ and /ʒ/** occur in loanwords [@cohen_loanword_2019]. They are written with a geresh: ו׳, ג׳, צ׳, ז׳.

## Vowels

| | Front | Central | Back |
|:--|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **High** | i | | u |
| **Mid** | e | | o |
| **Low** | | a | |

* Modern Hebrew has five vowels [@asherov_cohen_2019; @gafter_performing_2019].
* A yod after a vowel and not followed by one forms a diphthong, which is transcribed as a single unit: שַׁי /ˈʃ aj/, but בַּיִת /b a ˈj i t/.

# Alphabet

* Letters (graphemes) are shown without pointing unless a diacritic changes their value.
* *Dagesh* (the dot in a letter) distinguishes the stop from the fricative in ב, כ/ך and פ/ף. In other letters it marks historical gemination, which Modern Hebrew does not pronounce, and it is ignored.

| ה | /h/ | silent word-finally, with or without mapiq (מוֹרֶה /moˈᴚe/) |

## Shva and qamats: why the language is compromised

* **Shva.** The same sign, shva (ְ), marks both a vowelless consonant and a consonant followed by /e/, and spoken Hebrew does not follow the classical rules for which is which. The rules decide from the shape of the word: a shva is heard, for example, under the first of two like consonants (מָדַדְתִּי /madadeˈti/), under a prefix or a sonorant before another onset (לְבֵית /leˈvet/), and under the second of two shvas in a row (יִשְׁמְרוּ /jiʃmeˈᴚu/). Otherwise it is silent, which gives complex onsets as in קְטִיפָה /ktiˈfa/ [@asherov_batel_2019]. The word-initial conjunction ו 'and' is /ve/, as in spontaneous speech, even where the prescribed form is /u/ [@gafter_performing_2019]. These decisions come from the form of the word, not from the lexicon, so some words come out wrong. A meteg (ֽ) on a shva forces it to be heard.
* **Qamats qatan.** Qamats (ָ) is /a/ in most words but /o/ in some, such as חָכְמָה /ħoχˈma/, and the two look the same. The rules read a plain qamats as /o/ in only two cases: before a hataf qamats (צָהֳרַיִם /tsohoᴚaˈjim/), and in the frequent stem כל 'all', with or without a prefix (כָּל /ˈkol/, וְ|כָל /veˈχol/, but כָּלָה /kaˈla/). Elsewhere a qamats qatan is read as /o/ only when the text writes it with the separate sign ׇ (U+05C7), as he2ipa's diacritizers do but most texts do not: חׇכְמָה /ħoχˈma/.

# Syllable Structure

* Modern Hebrew allows complex onsets, including ones that arise from a silent shva (קְטִיפָה /ktiˈfa/) [@asherov_batel_2019].

# Lenition Rules

* Stop–fricative alternation: /b/–/v/, /k/–/χ/ and /p/–/f/ alternate. In pointed text the dagesh shows which one is used, so the rules follow it rather than predicting it. In Modern Hebrew the alternation is no longer fully predictable from position [@albert_2019].

# Misc. Rules

* **Maqaf.** Words joined by a maqaf (־) are transcribed as one word, with one stress: תֵּל־אָבִיב /tel ʔaˈviv/.
* **Patah gnuva.** A patah under a word-final ח or ע is pronounced before the consonant: שִׂיחַ /ˈsiaħ/, לֹעַ /ˈloaʕ/.
* **Stress** is final by default, or on the syllable before a patah gnuva (רוּחַ /ˈᴚuaħ/). Words with other stress need ole (U+05AB) on the stressed letter: מָדַ֫דְתִּי /maˈdadeti/ against unmarked /madadeˈti/. On Modern Hebrew stress, see @batel_cohen_silbervarod_2019.
* **Voicing assimilation** in obstruent clusters [@mizrachi_2019] is not transcribed.
* **Unstressed /a/** shows raising in current speech [@cohenpriva_gafter_2024]. This is below the level of the phoneme and is not transcribed.
